messages.mes:
*Cool wind moves through the rough grass around Alaric Red's boots.*

*The last thing that belongs to Earth is still there in memory—an old life, a world without visible mana, Classes, or this impossible second beginning. The present is different: the smell of soil and distant woodsmoke, an unfamiliar sky, and stone walls beyond the public road.*

*Alaric Red is already standing on an uncultivated roadside verge outside the nearby city. Cultivated fields and fenced holdings begin farther away. No one is close enough to have witnessed the instant of arrival.*

*The body is Human, healthy, and eighteen years old. Simple traveler's clothes are already being worn; a small pouch holding five silver rests at the belt. The memories are still from Earth.*

*A translucent interface opens across Alaric Red's vision.*

`SYSTEM INITIALIZATION COMPLETE`
`Origin: Earth`
`World: Avereth`
`Race: Human`
`Age: 18`
`Level: 1 | Rank: F`

`BASE STATS`
`STR 5 | VIT 5 | AGI 5 | INT 5 | PER 5 | WIL 5`

`Location: Public roadside verge outside Alderwatch, Valedorn Crown`
`Arrival Witnesses: NONE`
`Starting Possessions: Simple Traveler's Clothes | Small Pouch | 5 Silver`
`Local Common Language: Integrated`
`Mandatory Quest: NONE`

`CHARACTER CREATION — STEP 1/2`
`Choose your Base Class:`

`Warrior   — Favored Stats: STR / VIT`
`Mage      — Favored Stats: INT / WIL`
`Guardian  — Favored Stats: VIT / WIL`
`Duelist   — Favored Stats: STR / AGI`
`Ranger    — Favored Stats: AGI / PER`

`Your chosen Class immediately applies +1 to both Favored Stats at Level 1.`
`After choosing a Class, select exactly 2 Skills from that Class's Base Skill Pool.`

`Reply with your Class choice.`

*The System waits. Story time does not move during Character Creation.*

messages.mes:
The road took him at its own pace, a broad rutted track shared with carts and foot traffic that thinned as the walls rose ahead. Alderwatch announced itself first by smell — woodsmoke, dung, the river-damp tang of a market already running — then by sound: hammering from somewhere beyond the stone, dogs, a drover cursing a stubborn mule.

The western gate stood open. A pair of city watch leaned on their spears beneath it and watched the morning traffic with the boredom of men who had seen a thousand farmers and cared about none of them. One's gaze slid over Alaric's robes and staff without stopping. No one asked his name or business. He passed under the arch, the shade of it cool on his face, and came out into the city proper.

Alderwatch was stone and timber, three stories in places, laundry strung between upper windows. Wagons crowded the main street; a baker's boy wove past him with a basket on his hip, and somewhere a smith's rhythm rang steady as a heartbeat. He asked the way once — a woman beating a rug from a doorstep pointed without ceremony — and found the Guild by its sign: a crossed sword and branch over a wide door, painted boards worn at the edges but clean.

Inside, the hall was louder than the street. Morning light fell through high windows onto a long counter, notice boards thick with contract slips, and a scatter of adventurers — a bearded man in boiled leather arguing quietly over a map, two women checking gear by the wall, a hooded figure asleep in a corner bench. The floor was flagstone, scuffed by years of boots. A clerk, gray-haired, spectacles pushed up into thinning hair, stood behind the counter copying entries into a ledger, ink to his second knuckle.

She looked up as Alaric approached the counter. "Morning. Business or registration?"

"Red." She set the pen down and pulled a fresh page toward her, writing the name at the top in a quick, practiced hand. "Alaric Red. Spell it for me — no, never mind, that's plain enough."

She slid the ledger aside and reached beneath the counter, coming up with a flat stone the size of a dinner plate, its surface worn smooth and faintly scored with old marks. This she placed in front of him with both hands, the way one handles something heavier than it looks.

"Hand flat on the stone. It reads what you are — Class, Rank, that's all. No tricks in it, no records kept. The Guild's seen everything from farm boys to half-elves who lie about their age." She pushed her spectacles down onto her nose and waited, pen hovering over the ledger. "Age and place of origin, while you're at it, for the roll. You don't have to give the second if you'd rather not, but the age I need."

messages.mes:
The stone warmed under his palm. A breath, as she'd said — then a thin line of blue light traced itself across the smooth surface, curling into marks that meant nothing to the eye but plainly plenty to her.

"Mage." She leaned in over the counter for a second look, then sat back. "Well. That explains the staff." The light faded; the stone went dull and cool again as he lifted his hand. She wrote in the ledger — Class, Rank F, the age — her pen moving without hesitation.

"Mages are rarer walking in off the street than sword-arms, so you'll forgive me a second look." She blew across the wet ink, then reached under the counter again and brought up a thin brass badge on a cord, plain as a buckle, and a folded contract slip of Guild paper. She stamped the slip with the hall's seal, pressed the badge after it, and set both on the counter in front of him.

"Rank F, Mage. That badge is your standing in any recognized branch — don't lose it, replacing it costs you a day and a fee. The slip's a blank contract form, if you want work." She nodded toward the notice boards along the wall, thick with paper. "F-rank boards are the leftmost. Take what suits you, bring it to the counter, and it's yours — we mark it active, and when it's done you bring the proof back here for payout."

She took up her pen again and pulled the ledger back toward herself. "That's registration done. Anything else, or are you for the boards?"

The courtyard between the two buildings smelled of wet stone and horse; a pair of porters sat on a bench sharing bread, and a Guild man in a mud-splashed cloak came through the big doors at a jog, passing Alaric without a glance.

To the left a long counter was working — three adventurers leaning on it, arguing with a clerk about something written on a slip. To the right, tables, and the smell of spilled ale that never quite leaves a place like this. Ahead, on the far wall, hung the boards: rows of them, ranked by badges painted above each, and the leftmost was the smallest.

messages.mes:
The slip came free of its pin with a creak of the nail, and he carried it back across the hall floor to the long counter, past the three still arguing over their paperwork.

The clerk there — a broad woman with ink on her fingers and a badge of her own pinned crooked at her collar — took the slip, glanced at the heading, and glanced up at him.

"New face." She turned the slip over, then set it down on the counter between them instead of stamping it. "You're the one the annex stone read this morning — word travels about ten feet in this building. Mage, F-rank, straight off the street." She tapped the slip once. "Problem is, the stone only reads what you are. It doesn't make you a member. Membership's the two-silver fee — registration's not done until it's paid, and until it's paid I can't mark a contract active under your name. Guild rule, not mine."

She pushed the slip back toward him an inch, not unkindly.

"Pay the two silver here, I stamp you in, and this skeletons job is yours before the ink dries. Sixty copper from the temple wardens for the cull, that one — the galleries are an hour west, under the ruined chapel. Or walk away and think on it; the slip'll still be hanging when you've got coin to spare." She folded her hands and waited.

messages.mes:
Two silver coins crossed the counter, and the clerk swept them into the drawer without ceremony. She opened a ledger, wrote his name in a careful hand, and reached under the counter for a small tin box.

"Plate," she said, and set it before him: a flat rectangle of pale metal, stamped with the Guild's mark and his name, light as a coin. "Keep it on you. It's your standing at any branch on the continent — lose it, and replacing it costs a day and a fee. Rank changes get stamped here when you earn them."

Then she took the skeleton slip back, inked her stamp, and pressed it to the bottom corner. *ACTIVE.*

"There. First contract, Novice Red. Skeletons in the level 1 galleries, sixty copper from the temple wardens when it's turned in." She slid it across. "The catacombs sit under the ruined chapel an hour west, out the west gate. Ask the wardens at the chapel when you get there — they'll point you down. Bring proof the job's done to any Guild desk and they pay out."

She was already reaching for the next paper in her stack.

"Counter's where you turn in, same as where you take. Good luck down there."
